title: 5 ChatGPT Study Codes for Notes, Quizzes, and Test Prep
description:
Follow me and DM me "STUDY" on IG/FB only 👇

Secret ChatGPT codes for learning...

Choose your topic, paste one code into ChatGPT, and use the result for the part of studying you need.

1. /stickynotes
Creates sticky notes for the main points. Add any topic to turn its main points into a quick set of notes, so the key ideas sit in front of you before moving into the details.

2. /questionpredictor
Finds the 20% of information most likely to matter on a test. Add the topic you're studying and use the response to see which information deserves the most attention during your review.

3. /studyguide generate visual study image on this topic
Creates a visual diagram and a step-by-step explanation. The prompt asks ChatGPT to show the topic as an image, then break down the diagram so you work through it in order.

4. /quizme
Asks one question at a time and changes difficulty based on answers. Answer each question before moving on, and ChatGPT shapes the next question around your response.

5. /storymode
Turns the lesson into a story. Use this when you want the topic presented as a sequence you follow from one point to the next.

Use the same topic with each code to turn one lesson into 5 different study formats.

title: Why AI Benchmarks Don't Tell You If Your Product Works
description:
People use the word evals to mean two different things.

Model benchmarks like SWE-bench and GPQA Diamond tell you how good a model is in general. 

When you're building an AI product, you need evals that check whether your product actually does what you want it to do.

title: Giving AI a Credit Card Is Still Painful
description:
Join the AI Evals October 2026 cohort: https://maven.com/parlance-labs/evals?promoCode=yt-2026

If you're new to my channel, my name is Hamel Husain. I spent 20 years in data and machine learning at banks, startups, Airbnb, GitHub, before most people knew what any of that meant. In 2023 I started advising AI companies and noticed the same gap everywhere: nobody had a real way to test, measure, and improve their AI products. They were shipping on vibes.

So I started documenting how to fix that. What I built became the most popular evals course in the world: 4,500+ engineers and PMs from OpenAI, Google, Meta, Anthropic, and more. My colleague Shreya Shankar and I are also co-authoring the O'Reilly book on it.

This channel is where I share what I actually know about building AI products that hold up.

How I got here...
2003: Built credit-risk models right out of college (Math and Industrial Engineering). SQL, scripting, data visualization. The foundational stuff.
2005: Data consulting across a dozen industries. Reading messy data and finding where processes were broken. Same muscle I use now for error analysis on LLM products.
2008: Burned out and went to law school. Learned two things: I can write, and I'm an engineer who was kidding himself.
2010: Back to consulting. Predictive models across demand forecasting, marketing, and customer service.
2014: Joined DataRobot to sit near Kaggle grandmasters. Thousands of reps building predictive models fast.
2016: Data Scientist at Airbnb. Inherited a badly overfit growth model that had been running in prod. Helped set up systems so it couldn't happen again.
2017: Machine learning at GitHub. Led the team that built CodeSearchNet, a benchmark for semantic code search. Underneath, it was a set of evals for code understanding. OpenAI later used it to evaluate their first code embeddings, which became groundwork for the earliest coding models.
2022: Left to turn an open source developer tool into a company. ChatGPT shipped and the bet stopped making sense. I walked away.
2023: Independent consultant. Advised 50+ companies, startups to Fortune 500s. Everyone had the same gap: no real way to test or improve AI beyond vibe checks. I started documenting the fix.

This channel is the unfiltered version of what I've learned. What works, what doesn't, and how to build AI that actually holds up.

Hamel

title: 8 Claude Code skills I use for building better AI evals
description:
Join the AI Evals October 2026 cohort: https://maven.com/parlance-labs/evals?promoCode=yt-2026

Shipping an AI product is easy now. Knowing whether it actually works is still hard. The biggest mistake I see is teams writing evals before they've looked at a single real failure in their product.

Shreya Shankar and I built eight Claude Code skills to fix that. We shaped them by working with over 50 companies and teaching more than 5,000 students in our AI evals course. I walk through all eight, but most of the time goes to the two I'd start with. The first is error discovery, which builds a custom interface for reviewing your traces and keeps sampling new ones until you stop finding new failure modes. The second is the eval audit, which checks your setup against the mistakes we see most often. Get through those two and you'll be ahead of most people working on evals.

title: Program Overview: Welcome to Product Management
Webinar: What AI Can and Cannot Do: Intelligence Augmentation in Practice with Michael Bernstein
description:
- Explore these concepts in the AI-Powered Product Innovation course: https://bit.ly/pin-stf-webinar

- Browse all Stanford Online AI courses: https://online.stanford.edu/artificial-intelligence/courses-and-programs

Artificial intelligence is transforming how organizations approach problem-solving, decision-making, and innovation—but knowing where AI can create reliable value is just as important as knowing where it cannot.

In this Stanford Online webinar delivered in collaboration with Global Alumni, Professor Michael Bernstein explores the practical realities of AI adoption and the role of human judgment in an increasingly AI-enabled workplace. The session examines how to distinguish between problems AI can solve reliably and those that continue to require human expertise, judgment, and oversight.

Drawing on research and practical frameworks for human-AI interaction, Professor Bernstein explores how leaders and professionals can evaluate AI opportunities more thoughtfully, assess potential risks, and determine where AI can genuinely augment human capabilities.

title: Stanford CS153 Frontier Systems | Teaching AI to Touch Atoms
description:
For more information about Stanford's online Artificial Intelligence programs, visit: https://stanford.io/ai

Follow along with the course schedule and syllabus; visit: https://cs153.stanford.edu/

In this CS 153 Frontier Systems lecture, Periodic Labs cofounders Liam Ferriss and Dorje Chubak — veterans of OpenAI's post-training team and DeepMind's Genome project, respectively — walked students through their eleven-month-old mission to apply AI to the physical world, specifically using autonomous labs to accelerate the discovery of new materials including high-temperature superconductors. 

Operating out of a 40,000-square-foot Menlo Park facility where machine learning researchers work alongside physicists and chemists, their AI system (named Onnes, after the scientist who discovered superconductivity in 1908) runs a continuous loop of computational prediction, robotic synthesis, and experimental verification — closing the feedback cycle between digital intelligence and physical reality in a way no purely in-silico approach can. A key early lesson was abandoning their original plan of spending the first year purely computational: building smaller, semi-manual labs first allowed them to direct the research program and understand what to scale, faster. 

Dorje emphasized that the results of applying LLMs to actual atoms have exceeded even their own expectations, while Liam stressed that sample efficiency in reinforcement learning — not benchmark climbing — is the core technical frontier when physical experiments can't be arbitrarily scaled up the way digital rollouts can. They closed by pushing back on student anxiety about AGI displacing their careers, arguing that most scientific domains remain largely untouched by LLMs, that the bar to make meaningful AI-physical world progress is still surprisingly low, and that the history of civilization is essentially a materials story — making their work, in their view, among the highest-leverage bets anyone can make right now.

title: Build, Test, Deploy, Monitor: The Agent Development Lifecycle Explained
description:
Amy and Sean from LangChain break down the agent development lifecycle, the process agent engineers use to build and improve their agents. It comes down to four phases: build it in code with a framework like Deep Agents, test it with real inputs and expected outputs, deploy it into production, and monitor it with tracing and evals.

This is a clip from our full conversation where Amy and Sean answer the most commonly searched questions about AI agents, from the basics like what is an agent, what is RAG, and what is MCP, to harder questions like why agents hallucinate, how to evaluate them, and what LangChain actually does.

title: HTTP Channels for Managed Deep Agents
description:
Nathan Drezner, a product manager at LangChain, shows how to build a custom HTTP channel for a Managed Deep Agent so it can receive inbound requests from any service you don't control, like HubSpot, Salesforce, or a texting provider. He builds Reflex, an expense-reporting agent that receives receipt photos over iMessage through Photon, extracts the data, and stores it in durable memory backed by Context Hub. Along the way he covers writing verify and parse functions, managing thread IDs per user, sending replies with a post hook, checking the result in LangSmith, and when to reach for HTTP channels versus a custom UI on the LangGraph SDK.

title: Why Your AI Agent Fails in Production (And How to Catch It)
description:
Manual code  tweaking isn't a testing strategy. Here is how to actually evaluate AI agents for production. In this episode of AI Agent Clinic, Google Cloud engineer Dani Zamora and Matthew Feroz (Merge) take DocsHound, an open-source LangGraph agent, and build an end-to-end evaluation pipeline in 60 minutes.

🔗 Repositories & Resources:
• Open-Source Agent-Eval Toolkit (GitHub):  https://g.dev/cloud/agent-eval 
• DocsHound Agent Code: https://g.dev/cloud/docshound 
• Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Docs: https://g.dev/cloud/agent-evaluation 

Most autonomous loops look great in local demos but fail silently in production. In this hands-on clinic, we compress weeks of testing setup into one hour by:
1. Mapping agent execution flow and inner workings using Antigravity
2. Standardizing multi-turn traces with OpenTelemetry & OpenInference (making your evals work across agentic frameworks like ADK, LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, or custom implementations)
3. Pairing custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluation rubrics and deterministic checkers for quality and performance assessment
4. Additionally, tracking  signals like: latency, token usage, and API cost
5. Ensuring zero vendor lock-in by building on open-source standards

Along the way, our automated scorecard catches a blind spot: a 33% documentation quality score that while eye-balling the results we initially missed.

What exactly is an agent harness, and why is it the secret to fully autonomous coding? If your coding agents are hitting a wall, the problem might not be the model you are using, it might be the stack. In this episode of The Agent Factory, we break down how to stop relying on manual prompting and start building environments where AI can dynamically solve complex software engineering challenges.

First, we sit down with Ryan Lopopolo, the Google engineer who coined the term "agent harness". We will discuss why he hasn't manually written code since May, how to apply senior engineering principles to AI agents, and how agents are being deployed to operate Google Cloud. Then, Billy jumps into the code to demonstrate the difference between linear and closed-loop harnesses using the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Finally, Smitha reveals the three-layer stack you need to build high-performing agents today, featuring Gemini 3.8 Flash, Antigravity Boost, and the viral Google Skills GitHub repository.

Whether you are a developer trying to build your own agent loop, or a technical leader looking to scale AI autonomy across your infrastructure, you'll learn exactly how to configure the memory, tools, and guardrails necessary to make your agents reliable. You'll walk away with a clear understanding of when to use lightweight models for high-frequency loops, when to deploy orchestrators like Boost, and how to give your agents the precise domain knowledge they need to succeed.

Who's actually out there solving real, life-or-death problems with AI?

In this episode of The Agent Factory, host Luke Schlangen sits down with Bruno Farias de Souza, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of Neomed — a Brazilian healthtech startup using AI to optimize diagnostic imaging and cardiovascular data analysis. Bruno explains why AI won't replace physicians but will amplify them, how Neomed's machine learning models screen 150,000+ EKGs a month in under 7 seconds, and why "moving slow" is actually the fastest way to build trust — and save lives — in healthcare.
